title: K D Paul and Bisk Farm
subtitle: Krishnadas Paul, founder of Bisk Farm, connected a lifetime in trade with a new ambition in manufacturing and retained a lasting attachment to Kamarkita.
body:
From Kamarkita to commerce

Paul came from Kamarkita in the Burdwan region and moved to Kolkata with his father during his primary-school years. He died on 3 August 2020.[1]

His business education was rooted in a family enterprise. A retrospective account in Moneycontrol describes law studies followed by entry into the trading and distribution business his father had established in 1947. Following the division of that business among five brothers, Paul founded Aparna Agency in 1974, developing distribution relationships with established consumer-goods companies. This was not the background of a newcomer discovering commerce at retirement age: he brought decades of experience to his later venture.[2]

Distribution mattered because it placed the businessman between manufacturers, retailers and customers. That position offers a distinctive view of how a product becomes a habit: availability, price and trust must work together. Seen in this light, the move towards a proprietary brand was an expansion of Paul’s commercial world rather than a complete break with it.

Family landed society and enterprise

K. D. Paul belonged to the Pal household of Kamarkita, whose continuing ties were evident in its shared Durga Puja. Reporting after his death, Anandabazar Patrika identified Subrata Pal as a relative and Agnimitra Paul as a member of the household by marriage. Agnimitra, now West Bengal’s Minister-in-Charge of Urban Development, remembered him in 2020: “He had a deep attachment to the village.”[3],[4]

An older setting for the locality appears in Jnanendranath Kumar’s Bangsha-Parichay, volume XIV (1934). The book’s account of the Hitta-Burdwan branch conveys the scale of its former landed standing. It records a tradition that Uddhab Pal’s zamindari extended from the Damodar near Panagarh to the Bhagirathi near Katwa, while also describing losses during the Bargi raids and confiscation of jagirs after revenue arrears. It describes Radhakanta Pal’s extensive jagirs in Midnapore and Orissa, besides Burdwan, and preserves a story of revenue arriving at Hitta on elephants. The 1934 account specifically identifies Ayma Radhakantapur as a jagir then still in the possession of the Hitta Pals.

The same account offers a concrete connection between a landed family and urban business. After litigation depleted the Hitta family’s remaining property, Gopinath Pal established a rice business in Calcutta’s Barabazar and relieved his family’s financial difficulties. By 1934, Pashupatinath Pal was described as running the established iron and corrugated-sheet business, Gangnarayan Pal & Sons, in Barabazar’s Lohapatti. The narrative illustrates fortunes rebuilt through trade after estate losses, rather than a simple progression from landed surplus to industry.[5]

For K. D. Paul himself, the route to manufacturing began with his experience in the distribution business.

Building Bisk Farm

Bisk Farm began in 2000 with a biscuit factory at Uluberia, under SAJ Food Products. For Paul, who had spent decades in distribution, the venture brought the chance to build a brand of his own rather than sell only other manufacturers’ goods.[6]

In a 2015 interview with Outlook Business, he recalled suggesting a family biscuit company over dinner. His son-in-law Vijay Singh welcomed the idea. The early years brought heavy losses and weak brand recognition. When a takeover approach arrived in 2003, Paul discussed it with Singh and declined, choosing to preserve their brand’s identity.[7]

That choice did not remove the need to change. New advertising, operational adjustments and stronger distribution helped the business recover. The episode shows a combination of commitment and commercial judgement: Paul was prepared to risk capital on an independent venture, but also to revise its workings when the first approach failed.[8]

The village in the larger story

Residents credited Paul with improvements to lighting, water, schools and medical support. They also remembered his attention to the family Durga Puja while ill.[9]

Paul’s career gives a modern point of comparison for the enterprise described in these family histories: years spent building a distribution business, the decision to risk capital on a new brand and the judgement to change course when that brand struggled. These episodes resonate with the values of enterprise, sustained work and commercial judgement celebrated in Aguri family histories. His attachment to Kamarkita adds a further dimension, the responsibility of successful enterprise towards its place of origin.
